name: interpreter
intent: Define a representation for a small language's grammar - one expression type per rule - together with an interpret operation over a context, so that sentences of the language are evaluated by walking the tree the grammar forms.
problem: A program has to evaluate expressions in a small notation that keeps recurring - business rules, filters, formulas, query fragments, configuration expressions. Encoding each case as an ad-hoc if/else chain or as embedded host-language scripts makes the language impossible to extend, test or reason about, and every new rule edits the same growing function. The trigger is a grammar whose rules and their evaluation deserve to be first-class: named types or data cases plus one interpret operation, with the tree as the unit of composition.
context: Applies to small-to-medium grammars - the GoF book states the applicability limit explicitly - that are evaluated repeatedly and often composed by users or configuration. A parser (hand-written recursive descent, Pratt, or generated) typically builds the tree; the pattern then owns representation and evaluation, and the same tree can feed printing, checking or translation passes. It fits tool-adjacent and runtime-adjacent code (rule engines, query builders, template expressions, configuration DSLs), not full programming languages, which need parser generators, bytecode compilers and optimisers instead.
benefits: Grammar rules become named, independently testable units: terminal and nonterminal cases can be constructed directly in tests without parsing text first.
New rules are added by adding a node type (and one evaluator arm) rather than by editing a single growing conditional, so the change is local and reviewable.
One tree carries several operations - evaluate, print, type-check, optimise, translate - because the representation is separated from the processing.
The context object gives bindings, configuration and diagnostics a single explicit home, instead of threading ambient state through helper functions.
Composite structure: a nonterminal holds child expressions, so arbitrary nesting and reuse fall out of the tree shape (shared terminal nodes can even be interned Flyweight-style).
Failures have a natural granularity: each node returns a value or reports an error, so the diagnostic carries the sub-expression that caused it.
tradeoffs: One node type per grammar rule: a small grammar stays readable, but the type count grows with the language and the practical ceiling is a simple expression language.
Tree walking is the slowest evaluation strategy - no compilation, no constant folding, no bytecode - so hot expressions need a compiler pass, code generation or memoisation added on top.
The pattern says nothing about parsing, so a lexer and parser remain a second deliverable with its own edge cases, error reporting and testing burden.

Adding an operation is expensive while adding a rule is cheap: interpret lives on the nodes, so a new operation touches every node type unless the design is refactored to an external evaluator or a visitor.
Recursive evaluation spends stack per nesting level, which turns deeply nested or adversarial input into a denial-of-service surface and forces depth limits or an explicit work stack.
Interpreting free-form text is a security boundary of its own: untrusted rule input invites injection and resource exhaustion, and eval-like shortcuts are the classic mistake.

Node allocation and virtual dispatch dominate for high-frequency evaluation: each node is an object with children and a dispatch step, so the interpretation overhead can exceed the work the expression describes.

participants.responsibility: Declares the interpret(context) operation common to every node of the abstract syntax tree; the single interface the client and the nonterminals depend on.
Leaf node for a terminal symbol (literal, variable reference): implements interpret directly, without children, and is the recursion's base case.
Node for a grammar rule R ::= R1 ... Rn: holds one child expression per symbol and implements interpret by recursing into them, combining the results with the rule's own semantics.
Carries the information global to interpretation - variable bindings, configuration, diagnostics, output - and is passed to every interpret call so evaluation stays free of ambient state.
Builds (or is handed) the abstract syntax tree for a sentence and invokes interpret on its root; in practice the parser plus the calling application or service.

use_cases: Authorization and policy enforcement (Open Policy Agent / Rego): policies authored as rules like 'allow if input.method == "GET" and input.path starts with "/public"', compiled to an intermediate representation and evaluated against a request context — a production-scale Interpreter pattern deployed at cloud-native boundaries.

Secure workflow expressions (n8n, Camunda, Azure Logic Apps): end users author expressions like $json.customer.email in a graphical interface; the runtime evaluates these inside a V8 isolate or equivalent sandbox with memory and time budgets, preventing host access while supporting dot-notation navigation, arithmetic and boolean logic.

JMESPath query language evaluation: implementations in Go, Python, .NET and JavaScript parse a JMESPath expression into an AST of comparison, projection, function and identifier nodes; the TreeInterpreter recursively walks the tree against JSON data, exactly matching the Interpreter pattern's structure.

XPath 1.0/3.1 navigation against XML documents: libxml-rs (Rust) and Paligo/xee (Rust) implement XPath as a full lexer→parser→AST→eval pipeline where each AST node type (axis, node-test, predicate, function call) carries its own evaluation semantics against a context node and variable bindings.

Lightweight business rules (Easy Rules, JMX RuleEngine): rules defined as annotated POJOs or YAML with condition expressions and action callbacks; the RulesEngine evaluates conditions by traversing an expression tree and fires matching actions — an Interpreter-lite pattern without a full Rete network.

JSONPath filtering with expression extensions (jsonpath-ng, python-jsonpath): JSONPath expressions with arithmetic and binary comparison operators are parsed into expression-object AST nodes that support evaluation against JSON documents, with extensions for filter predicates that are themselves small expression trees.

Feature-flag targeting expressions (LaunchDarkly, Unleash): targeting rules like 'country in ["US","UK"] and percentage > 50' are parsed into Boolean expression trees evaluated per evaluation request; the same tree structure is reused across SDK evaluation, bucketing and JSON serialization.

Business rule DSLs in BRMS and rule engines (Drools, Easy Rules): rules authored by non-engineers at runtime such as 'IF customer.tier == "gold" AND order.total > 500 THEN discount = 0.15', evaluated against a data context per request.

Query predicate DSLs with Boolean operators and field comparisons (status:active AND priority:high OR assignee:john), parsed into expression trees and evaluated against collections or translated to SQL/LINQ.
Feature-flag targeting rules and access policies (enable: when env=prod and rollout > 50%), interpreted at load time or per decision request.

Formula and template languages in spreadsheets, report generators and low-code builders where end users author expressions (e.g., Jinja2, Handlebars, Mustache parse template syntax into ASTs of variable substitutions and control-flow nodes).
Configuration DSLs with conditional logic (Terraform HCL, nginx directives, Apache .htaccess), evaluated at load time to produce runtime behaviour from declarative files.
Regular expression engines and glob matchers: patterns like (a|b)*c are parsed into ASTs of Concatenation, Alternation, KleeneStar and Literal nodes, then evaluated against input strings.
ORM and query-builder expression trees (Entity Framework Core, Hibernate criteria API, LINQ): the tree is translated to SQL rather than evaluated in-process.
Search and filter DSLs (Elasticsearch query DSL, GitHub code search, Lucene query parser): user search strings are parsed into must/should/must_not trees evaluated against indexed documents.
Command and robot instruction languages (G-code, drawing primitives, network protocol control words) where one-byte instruction words must map to typed actions via an explicit grammar.

Front ends of compilers, linters and static analysers: the same AST carries evaluation, pretty-printing, type-checking and optimisation passes — the Interpreter is the evaluation layer over a tree built by a separate parser.

Embedded authorization and routing expressions (Common Expression Language/CEL): applications parse and type-check a CEL expression once into an AST, then evaluate that stored tree repeatedly with request-specific variable bindings, making a small, portable policy DSL a direct compile-once/evaluate-many Interpreter use case.

Safe application expressions (Symfony ExpressionLanguage): the component parses expressions into a ParsedExpression AST whose nodes are evaluated against supplied variables or compiled for reuse, fitting small configuration and authorization DSLs without executing arbitrary host-language text.

Policy modules (HashiCorp Sentinel): modules are parsed into ASTs and the runtime walks imported module trees during policy evaluation, with lazy and memoized rule semantics over an explicit policy scope.
avoid_when: The grammar is large or the language has real syntax: use a generated or hand-written parser plus an AST library (yacc/bison, ANTLR, Racc, a recursive-descent or Pratt parser) and keep this pattern for the evaluator only.
Only two or three simple expressions will ever exist: a switch expression, a lookup table or a dispatch table is smaller and clearer than a node hierarchy.

The expression language is already a subset of the host language: reuse the host's own AST and evaluator (Python's ast with a node whitelist, .NET expression trees, a Lua or WASM sandbox) instead of re-implementing it, and never call eval on untrusted text.
Evaluation sits in a performance-critical inner loop: compile or generate code instead of walking a tree on every call.
Input is untrusted and unbounded: without a depth limit, a step budget and a sandbox, an interpreter is a resource-exhaustion vector.
The variation is one algorithm over fixed data rather than a grammar - that is strategy or a dispatch table, not interpreter.
anti_patterns: Letting the same node also tokenise or parse text: representation, parsing and evaluation are three concerns, and mixing them recreates the coupling the pattern removes.
Growing the grammar without a completeness check (no exhaustive match, no sealed set, no final classes): a missing rule then fails at run time on the input that needs it.
Evaluating with ambient global state instead of an explicit context, so results depend on call order and cannot be reproduced in tests.

Expression Language Injection (CWE-917): passing unvalidated user input directly into an expression evaluator — even a whitelist-based one — can enable remote code execution when attackers craft inputs that exploit double-resolution, reflection chains, or prototype pollution. Always isolate user-authored expressions in a sandboxed process with no host access.

Sandbox escape via operator overloading or method hijacking: when user data is wrapped in proxy objects (for safe dot-notation access), a malicious expression can sometimes call unexpected methods on those proxies, bypassing isolation. Audit every exposed method and use monomorphic dispatch, not dynamic method lookup.

Prototype-pollution attacks on expression results: a malicious expression can add or mutate __proto__ or Object.prototype properties in the evaluation result, corrupting downstream consumers. Sanitize all computed object keys and reject object literal mutations that affect the prototype chain.
Re-parsing the same expression on every evaluation: parsing is expensive; high-frequency evaluation demands a cached AST. Re-parsing each request is a silent performance bug, not a design feature.

Left-recursive grammars in a hand-written recursive-descent parser: a rule R ::= R + E written as a direct recursive descent loops forever. Rewrite left-recursive rules using iterative precedence-climbing or an explicit stack.

Mutable expression nodes in a shared tree: when the same node appears in multiple branches and per-evaluation mutations corrupt it, the tree is no longer reusable or reentrant. Nodes must be immutable or uniquely owned.

Keeping the class-per-rule structure after the grammar outgrows it: dozens of nearly-identical expression classes for a grammar that now needs precedence levels, backtracking and error recovery means it is time to switch to a generated parser plus bytecode compiler.

Unbounded recursion over untrusted input: no depth limit, no step budget and no sandbox makes the interpreter a resource-exhaustion surface. A tiny adversarial expression (10,000 nested ANDs) can crash the process.
Confusing Interpreter with parser: one hierarchy that both tokenises text and evaluates trees couples two independently-changing concerns and recreates the coupling the pattern removes.

Interpreter as one giant if/else chain over node strings: no rule is testable in isolation, no tool can see the grammar, and adding a rule touches the same growing function that every other rule touches.

Adding an operation is expensive while adding a rule is cheap: when the operation set (evaluate, print, type-check, optimise) grows faster than the grammar, refactor to an external Visitor or a data-driven evaluator dispatch to avoid touching every node type for every new operation.

Type-unsafe context maps: storing variable bindings in a generic map (dict, HashMap) and looking them up with string keys at evaluation time defeats the type system's ability to catch typos; prefer typed Context with known fields or a sealed union of binding types.

eval() shortcuts: evaluating user-supplied text with the host language instead of a whitelisted interpreter, turning a bounded rule language into remote code execution. The Interpreter pattern is the safe, auditable alternative — it only understands the operations you explicitly implement.

design_principles: Separation of concerns: grammar representation, parsing and evaluation are three separate problems; the pattern owns representation and evaluation.
Open/closed principle: new grammar rules arrive as new node types and evaluator arms, and existing rules stay closed for modification.
Composition over inheritance: a nonterminal composes its child expressions (Composite), which is what makes arbitrary nesting possible.
Single responsibility: each node knows one grammar rule's semantics and nothing about the rest of the tree.
Explicit context over ambient state: bindings and configuration travel in a Context parameter, keeping evaluation reproducible and testable.
Fail fast at the type level: prefer a checked-complete node set (sealed, enum, union) so a missing rule is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise.
Grammar as the spec, not the code: write the grammar in BNF first; the class hierarchy is a direct codification of it, not an independent design decision.
Fail fast at the type boundary: prefer sealed/enum/final types with exhaustive matching so a missing rule is a compile error, not a runtime surprise on the input that needs it.
Evaluation is a pure function of tree + context: no side effects in interpret() unless the language intentionally models them; side-effect-free evaluation is trivially cacheable and reentrant.
Parser–interpreter seam is sacred: never let evaluation look at source text; never let the parser perform interpretation. They are developed, tested and versioned independently.
best_practices: Design the grammar first in BNF or a formal notation before writing any class — the grammar IS the design, and a clear grammar makes the node hierarchy obvious.

Keep the node set closed and machine-checked: sealed hierarchy (Java 17+, Kotlin), final classes (C++, Java), discriminated union (Rust, TypeScript), or exhaustive pattern matching (Python match/case). A new rule then breaks the build instead of failing at runtime.

Separate parsing from interpretation strictly: the parser is a distinct component that produces the tree; evaluation never touches text. This lets you swap a hand-written recursive-descent parser for a generated one without touching any expression class.

Pass an explicit Context (bindings, options, diagnostics) into every interpret() call; keep evaluation free of global or ambient state so nodes are reusable, reentrant, and testable against any context.
Add depth and step counters to the Context and abort evaluation when limits are exceeded — protects against stack overflow on adversarial or machine-generated deeply nested input.

Prefer iterative evaluation for flat chains of commutative operators (MultiAnd, MultiOr): flatten children into a list and fold with all()/any() instead of nesting recursively, so depth is O(1) rather than O(chain length).
Short-circuit AND/OR so a false left child of AND (or true left child of OR) skips the right subtree — essential when right-side evaluation has side effects or can fail.
Return typed results or explicit error values from interpret(); avoid signalling ordinary evaluation failures with exceptions, panics, or sentinel values the caller must guess.
Cache and reuse parsed ASTs: parsing is expensive; once built, a tree can be evaluated against many contexts. For high-frequency evaluation, compile the AST to bytecode or a callable delegate.
Make expression nodes immutable (frozen data classes, final fields, readonly properties): shared subtrees used in multiple places must never be corrupted by per-evaluation mutations.

Test rules as data first — construct trees directly in unit tests without parsing — and add a thin parser suite covering the textual surface; this gives fast isolated tests for both tree structure and grammar.
Whitelist all operators and symbols from user input; never pass an operator string directly to a native comparison or eval — always validate against a known safe set.
Share or intern repeated terminal nodes (Flyweight) to avoid aliasing bugs when the same literal appears in multiple branches of the tree.

Pre-compile expressions to delegates or bytecode for hot paths: tools like FastExpressionCompiler (C#) or GraalVM/Truffle can compile an expression tree to native code, turning O(n) tree-walk into a single function call — apply when latency budgets are tight and the same expression is evaluated thousands of times.

Isolate untrusted expressions in a sandboxed VM (V8 isolate, WebAssembly sandbox, subprocess): enforce memory caps, time budgets and no file/network access; never evaluate user input in the host process even with a whitelist — expression language injection (CWE-917) turns a single unsafe eval into remote code execution.

Audit the operator surface: every named operator or function in the grammar is a potential injection vector; prefer typed, closed function registries over string-dispatched operators that resolve at runtime from a context map.

Version the grammar explicitly: when the grammar evolves, version the AST nodes (e.g., v1.Equal vs v2.Equal) so that cached trees from older inputs can be detected and rejected or migrated before evaluation.

https://openpolicyagent.org/docs/policy-language — Open Policy Agent (OPA) Rego: a Datalog-inspired declarative policy language whose evaluation model maps directly to the Interpreter pattern, with rule bodies evaluated against variable bindings and a Context carrying input/data/global scopes.

https://github.com/open-policy-agent/opa/blob/main/internal/planner/planner.go — OPA Rego query planner: converts Rego queries into an executable intermediate representation (IR) plan of blocks and statements, a two-stage parse-then-plan architecture that cleanly separates grammar representation from evaluation.

https://symfony.com/doc/current/expression_language.html — Symfony ExpressionLanguage component: a safe, typed expression language for PHP and Twig with an explicit AST-based evaluator, whitelist-only operators, and no eval on untrusted input.

https://owasp.org/www-community/vulnerabilities/Expression_Language_Injection — OWASP Expression Language Injection (CWE-917): attacker-controlled input fed to an EL interpreter can yield remote code execution; covers Spring JSP double-resolution risks and mitigation (springJspExpressionSupport=false).

https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/ef2f21fe/packages/@n8n/expression-runtime/README.md — n8n expression-runtime: a three-layer secure evaluator (Runtime/V8 isolate, Bridge, Evaluator) with 128 MB memory cap, AST security hooks (ThisSanitizer, PrototypeSanitizer, DollarSignValidator), and lazy proxy-based data access.

https://github.com/jmespath/go-jmespath/blob/master/interpreter.go — go-jmespath TreeInterpreter: a concrete tree-walk interpreter for JMESPath expressions that recursively processes AST nodes against JSON data, illustrating the Interpreter pattern applied to a real-world query language.

https://docs.rs/libxml-rs/latest/libxml_rs/xml/xpath/index.html — libxml-rs XPath module: a complete XPath 1.0 engine in Rust with explicit AST, lexer, parser, context, and eval modules, demonstrating the Interpreter pattern in a systems-programming context.

https://github.com/EasyRules/easyrules — Easy Rules (j-easy/easyrules): a lightweight Java rules engine using an Interpreter-like pattern where Rule encapsulates condition+action, Facts carry evaluation context, and RulesEngine coordinates sequential rule firing.

https://deviq.com/design-patterns/rules-engine-pattern/ — DevIQ Rules Engine Pattern: externalizes business rule logic from core code; contrasts lightweight Interpreter-style evaluation with full Rete-network production systems (Drools).

https://doi.org/10.1145/3622808 — Larose, Vollmer & Marr, 'AST vs. Bytecode: Interpreters in the Age of Meta-Compilation' (OOPSLA 2023): empirical study finding AST and bytecode interpreters perform similarly after JIT optimization; self-optimizing ASTs can close the gap, relevant for high-frequency expression evaluation.

https://stefan-marr.de/2023/10/ast-vs-bytecode-interpreters/ — Stefan Marr blog summary of AST vs bytecode interpreter study: bytecode does not inherently outperform AST when both are well-optimized; AST interpreters benefit from self-optimization and meta-compilation frameworks (GraalVM, RPython).

https://github.com/dadhi/FastExpressionCompiler — FastExpressionCompiler (FEC) for C# expression trees: 10–40× faster compilation than Expression.Compile with lower memory use; relevant for high-frequency Interpreter pattern evaluation where compile-to-delegate replaces tree-walk.

https://softwarepatternslexicon.com/haskell/case-studies/building-a-compiler-or-interpreter/ — Software Patterns Lexicon: 'Building a Compiler or Interpreter in Haskell' — functional programming approach using Parsec/Megaparsec for parsing and a monadic evaluator for the Interpreter pattern, demonstrating separation of grammar (AST data types) from evaluation (monadic interpret function).

https://www.cs.tufts.edu/comp/150FP/archive/jamie-willis/parsing-patterns.pdf — 'Design Patterns for Parser Combinators (Functional Pearl)': survey of reusable combinator patterns for building parsers that produce ASTs consumed by an Interpreter; relevant for understanding how parser combinators and the Interpreter pattern compose.

https://stefan-marr.de/downloads/oopsla23-larose-et-al-ast-vs-bytecode-interpreters-in-the-age-of-meta-compilation.pdf — Full PDF of the OOPSLA 2023 AST vs bytecode study (Larose et al.): covers RPython and GraalVM meta-compilation contexts, self-optimizing ASTs, and memory trade-offs between tree-walk and bytecode evaluation.

https://design-patterns-case-study.readthedocs.io/en/latest/interpreter_pattern.gen.html — canonical Interpreter pattern mapping: grammar rules become expression nodes, sentences form an AST, and interpret(context) evaluates terminal and nonterminal expressions.
https://cel.dev/overview/cel-overview — Common Expression Language: expressions are parsed and checked into an AST, then evaluated repeatedly with variable and function bindings.
https://symfony.com/doc/current/expression_language.html — Symfony ExpressionLanguage: parses to a ParsedExpression AST, supports node evaluation, and can compile expressions for reuse.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/sentinel/docs/extending/internals — Sentinel internals: modules are parsed into ASTs and the interpreter walks them during policy evaluation.

https://homepages.cwi.nl/~jurgenv/papers/TOOLS2011.pdf — Hills, Klint, van der Storm & Vinju, “A Case of Visitor versus Interpreter Pattern”: empirical comparison found Visitor more maintainable in most realistic maintenance scenarios, a caution when the operation set grows.
